introduction-the-meeting-that-never-ends.core: Decisions stall between two failure modes: one person decides without buy-in, or everyone must agree and nobody can. Good consensus frameworks get both speed and commitment.

first_principles.problem: A team debates on-call rotations for six weeks of meetings. Or a manager decides alone, and engineers quietly resist the result.

analogy.title: A family choosing a holiday
analogy.story: If one parent books alone, others sulk. If everyone must agree, no holiday gets booked. A good process gathers wishes, then someone decides.
analogy.breaks: Families are small. Engineering decisions affect many teams, so structure matters more.

example.title: Six weeks on a CI tool

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Decision made with input and buy-in.

check.q: What are the two failure modes of group decisions?
check.a: One person deciding without buy-in, and requiring everyone to agree so nothing gets decided.

why-engineers-need-consensus-frameworks.core: Engineering is decision-making; stalled decisions block everything downstream. Frameworks make the who, how and when of decisions explicit so teams keep moving.

first_principles.problem: A REST-vs-gRPC choice drags on; sprints slip, people context-switch and momentum dies while the code waits.
truths: Code is the output of decisions.
derivation: Treat decisions as **work items** with owners and deadlines.

analogy.title: A traffic junction without lights
analogy.story: Every driver waits for everyone else; nobody goes. Lights (rules) let traffic flow.
analogy.breaks: Traffic rules are universal. Decision rules must be set per team or company.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Teams resume work the following Monday.

check.q: Why are stalled decisions so costly?
check.a: All work that depends on them waits, and teams lose momentum and context.

nemawashi-the-art-of-the-pre-meeting.core: Nemawashi ("digging around the roots") means talking to stakeholders one-on-one before the meeting: hearing concerns, adjusting the proposal and building support, so the meeting confirms rather than fights.

first_principles.problem: Proposals unveiled in a big meeting get ambushed by objections nobody heard before, and the meeting ends with 'let's discuss more'.
truths: People raise concerns more honestly one-on-one.
derivation: Meet each **individually** to share the draft and hear concerns.
Use the meeting to **confirm**, not debate.

analogy.title: Transplanting a tree
analogy.story: Gardeners dig carefully around the roots for weeks before moving a big tree, so it survives the move.
analogy.breaks: Trees don't negotiate. People may change their minds later, so document agreements.

example.title: Proposing a new on-call model

steps.label: Value
steps.detail: A concern found early became a design improvement.

example.outcome: the decision meeting is short and positive.

check.a: Digging around the roots, from preparing a tree for transplanting.

the-spade-framework-structuring-the-deci.core: SPADE (Gokul Rajaram, Square) structures a decision: Setting (what, when, why), People (who's consulted, who approves, the single decider), Alternatives, Decide, Explain. It removes ambiguity about who decides.

first_principles.problem: Decisions stall because nobody knows who has the final say, and the alternatives weren't laid out clearly.
derivation: **Setting**: precise what, deadline, why it matters.
**Alternatives**: realistic options with pros and cons.

analogy.title: A jury with a judge
analogy.story: Many people give input, but the process and who rules are clear before the trial begins.
analogy.breaks: Trials have legal rules. SPADE works only if the group agrees to it before starting.

example.title: Choosing a message broker

steps.label: Clarity
steps.detail: Everyone knows who decides and when.

example.outcome: a fast decision with visible reasoning.

check.q: What does each letter in SPADE stand for?

disagree-and-commit-the-essential-comple.core: Once a decision is made through a fair process, everyone commits to making it work, even those who disagreed. Disagreement belongs before the decision, not in quiet resistance after it.

first_principles.problem: Losing parties slow-walk implementation or relitigate the decision, so the organisation pays for a choice without getting its benefits.
truths: Disagreement before the decision improves it.
derivation: Allow revisiting only with **new information** or at agreed checkpoints.

analogy.title: A sports team's play call
analogy.story: Players can argue in the huddle, but once the play is called everyone runs it at full effort.
analogy.breaks: Games end quickly. Engineering decisions play out over months, so set review points.

example.title: Losing the database debate
example.scenario: An engineer preferred MongoDB; Postgres was chosen.

steps.label: Trust
steps.detail: Review checkpoint means disagreement isn't ignored forever.

example.outcome: the decision gets a fair test.

check.q: When is it legitimate to reopen a decision?
check.a: When significant new information emerges or at a pre-agreed review point.

nemawashi-spade-the-complete-decision-li.core: Combine the three: Nemawashi to prepare and gather input, SPADE to structure and make the decision, and disagree-and-commit to execute together. Each covers a different stage.

first_principles.problem: Teams use one technique and still stall: pre-meetings without a decider, or a decider without buy-in, or a decision nobody commits to.
truths: Decisions have before, during and after phases.
Each phase has distinct failure modes.
derivation: **After**: disagree and commit, with a review date.

analogy.title: A wedding
analogy.story: Months of conversations with families (preparation), a ceremony with clear roles (decision), then the commitment to make it work (execution).
analogy.breaks: Weddings are one-offs. Decision processes should become lightweight habits.

example.title: Moving to a monorepo

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: A contentious change lands with broad support.

example.outcome: decisions are prepared, made and executed well.

check.a: Nemawashi: one-on-one preparation and input gathering.
